summary:
Osmaniye province has no trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme or local institution in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Osmaniye stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which applies here without local modification.

The baseline national position is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Legislative pressure has been sustained. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as among the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; LGBT activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International recorded three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. None of the three was submitted to parliament. In 2026 the draft package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed, and a February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years in prison; that measure was not included in the 12th judicial package.

Enforcement has not waited for legislation. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans Pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Association and expression are also constrained. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that these could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof, and risk their "unfit report" leaking publicly.

Transition-related care is restricted. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, part of the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.
tangentialFactors:
The national backdrop a trans visitor carries into Osmaniye includes documented street-level and custodial risk. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken off the record.

Checkpoint interaction is the principal outing vector. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway.

Violence remains lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Custody conditions add a further layer. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Türkiye since 1988, but the pathway operates within a Health Ministry apparatus that has recently tightened. A regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, which risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Residents under 21 are affected by the June 2025 ban from the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency on the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures.

No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no statutory discrimination remedy, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Conscripts who declare homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must supply photographic proof, and may see their "unfit report" circulate publicly. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from service.

Organising carries dissolution risk: an İzmir court ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved in December 2025 over social-media images said to encourage or promote LGBTI identities. Complaints by LGBT detainees are described as ineffective and capable of attracting further violence, and there is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Osmaniye-specific source on policing, pride events, clinics, shelters or civil-society presence was located for this record; the province-level findings rest entirely on the national framework and on reporting from Istanbul, İzmir, Ankara and Kayseri. Whether Osmaniye authorities have applied the national GBT checkpoint practice is unresolved.

The status of the three draft law packages made public during 2025 is stated in the sources as not submitted to parliament, and the 2026 removal of the draft package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions is recorded as a single-source claim requiring confirmation against the final text of the 12th judicial package.

The February 2026 proposal criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" is reported as not included in the 2026 omnibus bill; whether it remains under consideration elsewhere in the legislative process is not sourced here.

Whether the June 2025 hormone ban for under-21s has been challenged in court, and whether it applies to visitors obtaining medication privately, is not addressed in the inventory.

The number of people stopped in the Beyoğlu checkpoint reporting is given as approximate, and the Article 5 European Convention argument is attributed to legal experts cited in that reporting rather than to a court ruling.
